The second phrase is “good and regular.” In BCO 20-3 (cf. BCO 24-3), “all communing members in good and regular standing, but no others, are entitled to vote in the churches to which they are respectively attached." Good standing focuses on those who are free

artifacts.synopsis: Mr. Psiaki complained that Covenant Presbyterian Church's Session erred in installing officers elected at a congregational meeting that excluded communicant members under age 18 from voting, in violation of the BCO. The SJC sustained the complaint (15-5), holding that all communicant members have a constitutional right to vote in officer elections regardless of age, and that church bylaws may not override BCO provisions; multiple dissenting opinions argued that BCO 20-3 and 24-3's phrase 'good and regular standing' permits local sessions to establish reasonable minimum voting ages.

artifacts.synopsis: TE Tolivar Wills complained that Metro Atlanta Presbytery improperly dissolved Grace North Atlanta Church without following formal judicial process under BCO 40-6. The SJC denied the complaint, ruling that BCO 13-9(f) grants presbytery inherent authority to dissolve a church without mandating any specific procedure, and that the record did not demonstrate clear error in MAP's exercise of its discretion and judgment.

artifacts.title: Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery (2007-09 & 2007-10)
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained two consolidated complaints by TE Eliot Lee against Korean Eastern Presbytery, annulling KEP's actions in empowering a Pulpit (Stated Supply Approval) Commission to act on behalf of the HKPC session without congregational consent, and annulling KEP's filing of a civil lawsuit in New Jersey state court to adjudicate ecclesiastical matters. The opinion extensively discusses the non-hierarchical nature of PCA polity and the limits of a presbytery's authority over local congregations.

artifacts.title: Constitutionality of GA directive to omit financial amounts from presbytery minutes
artifacts.disposition: advice given — action partially constitutional, editing of record unconstitutional

matches.evidence: The CCB advised that directing presbyteries to omit financial amounts from call-change records was constitutional as an exercise of GA oversight, but any actual editing of an already-adopted minute record was unconstitutional.
